name.text: 01 Question: Architecture of Distributed Git Repositories

questiontext.text: <p>In a distributed Git workflow, what is the key functional distinction between `origin` and `upstream` remotes?</p>

answer.text: <p>`origin` refers to your personal fork of the repository on GitHub where you push work, while `upstream` points to the authoritative central project repository from which you fetch updates.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Correct. In fork-and-pull workflows, `origin` is your personal remote fork, and `upstream` is the central project repository.</p>

answer.text: <p>`origin` is stored on your local hard drive, whereas `upstream` is stored in the computer's CPU cache.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Both `origin` and `upstream` are network remotes hosted on GitHub or another server.</p>

answer.text: <p>`origin` only accepts text files, whereas `upstream` only accepts digital image files.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Git remotes track all file formats committed to the repository.</p>

answer.text: <p>`origin` is deleted automatically whenever a pull request is merged.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Remote repository pointers persist indefinitely until manually deleted.</p>

name.text: 02 Question: Anatomy of a Git Merge Conflict

questiontext.text: <p>When Git encounters conflicting edits in a file during a merge, what does the text between `<<<<<<< HEAD` and `=======` represent?</p>

answer.text: <p>The local changes present on the currently checked-out branch before the merge was attempted.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Correct. `<<<<<<< HEAD` marks the start of the current branch's code, while `=======` separates it from the incoming changes up to `>>>>>>>`.</p>

answer.text: <p>The remote changes made by another developer on GitHub.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Incoming changes appear between `=======` and `>>>>>>>`.</p>

answer.text: <p>A fatal virus warning generated by the Linux kernel.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Conflict markers are standard Git notification delimiters.</p>

answer.text: <p>An encrypted cryptographic hash representing the author's password.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Conflict markers contain human-readable plaintext from the conflicted branches.</p>

name.text: 03 Question: Adjudicating Conflicts in TEI XML

questiontext.text: <p>Why is simply choosing 'Accept Current' or 'Accept Incoming' in a merge conflict tool dangerous in TEI XML documents?</p>

answer.text: <p>Because both branches may contain valid, complementary editorial markup (e.g. one editor added a gloss while the other corrected an apparatus pointer) that must be merged rather than discarded.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Correct. Editorial conflicts in digital scholarship frequently require synthesising contributions from both branches rather than arbitrarily discarding one editor's scholarly work.</p>

answer.text: <p>Because clicking either button triggers an immediate irreversible format of the user's hard drive.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Git never damages physical hardware.</p>

answer.text: <p>Because XML schemas automatically crash if both versions are not identical.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Schemas evaluate validity of the resolved result, not previous versions.</p>

answer.text: <p>Because GitHub bans user accounts that resolve conflicts in under five minutes.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. GitHub imposes no time restrictions on conflict resolution.</p>

questiontext.text: <p>What command-line operation should an editor immediately execute after editing a conflicted TEI file to verify basic syntax before staging?</p>

answer.text: <p>`xmllint --noout <filename>.xml`</p>

feedback.text: <p>Correct. `xmllint --noout` quickly verifies that manual resolution did not leave unclosed tags, unbalanced brackets, or orphan conflict markers.</p>

answer.text: <p>`rm -rf .git`</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. That disastrously deletes the entire Git repository history!</p>

answer.text: <p>`git push --force origin main`</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Force-pushing unverified or broken files corrupts the shared repository.</p>

answer.text: <p>`ping google.com`</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Testing network connectivity does not validate XML file syntax.</p>

questiontext.text: <p>What primary protection does a Continuous Integration (CI) pipeline (such as GitHub Actions) provide for a collaborative scholarly edition?</p>

answer.text: <p>It automatically runs schema validation and test suites on every pushed commit and pull request, preventing invalid XML or broken code from ever being merged into `main`.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Correct. CI acts as an automated quality gate, ensuring that all contributed files strictly conform to project schemas before merging.</p>

answer.text: <p>It prints the edition on physical paper and mails it to the university library.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. CI is an automated cloud-based software build and testing system.</p>

answer.text: <p>It generates artificial student grades to reduce instructor marking workloads.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. CI tests code and document validity, not academic student grading.</p>

answer.text: <p>It renames all files with random numbers to improve cybersecurity.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. CI maintains established file naming conventions.</p>

name.text: 06 Question: ISO Schematron vs Grammar Schemas

questiontext.text: <p>Why do mature TEI projects pair Relax NG grammars with ISO Schematron rules in their validation sweeps?</p>

answer.text: <p>Relax NG enforces structural grammar and element hierarchies, while Schematron enforces cross-element constraints and business rules (e.g., verifying that every `@wit` points to a declared `<witness>`).</p>

feedback.text: <p>Correct. Grammar schemas define valid parent-child structures, whereas Schematron uses XPath to validate relational constraints across distinct parts of the document.</p>

answer.text: <p>Schematron is used solely to compress XML files into ZIP archives.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Schematron is a rule-based validation language, not a compression algorithm.</p>

answer.text: <p>Relax NG only works on Windows, while Schematron only works on Mac.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Both validation standards are cross-platform and open-source.</p>

answer.text: <p>Because university accreditation requires using at least two different software licenses.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Both tools are open standards used for complementary technical verification.</p>

name.text: 07 Question: Etiquette and Rigor in Pull Request Reviews

questiontext.text: <p>Which practice exemplifies rigorous scholarly peer review within a GitHub Pull Request?</p>

answer.text: <p>Reviewing line-by-line diffs against the primary witness facsimile, testing validation locally, and providing constructive commentary explaining why specific markup choices need revision.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Correct. Scholarly peer review combines evidentiary verification against primary sources with polite, actionable critique of code and markup.</p>

answer.text: <p>Approving all pull requests immediately without reading the changed files.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Rubber-stamping PRs defeats the quality-control purpose of peer review.</p>

answer.text: <p>Posting abusive comments criticizing the other student's personal handwriting.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Professional academic collaboration requires respectful, constructive discourse.</p>

answer.text: <p>Deleting the pull request branch without providing any feedback.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Unilateral deletion without explanation disrupts collaborative teamwork.</p>

questiontext.text: <p>Why is making small, 'atomic' commits with informative commit messages superior to committing an entire month of changes at once?</p>

answer.text: <p>Atomic commits isolate discrete logical changes, making it straightforward to review diffs, identify when regressions occurred, or revert specific defects without losing other work.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Correct. Atomic commits preserve a transparent, auditable history where individual changes can be tested, tracked, or reverted cleanly.</p>

answer.text: <p>Because Git charges a financial fee for every commit that exceeds 100 lines of text.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Git is free and open-source software with no per-commit fees.</p>

answer.text: <p>Because computers run out of RAM if a commit contains more than two files.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Git handles commits with thousands of files easily, but large commits hinder human review.</p>

answer.text: <p>Because GitHub automatically rejects any commit message longer than five words.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. GitHub supports multi-line, detailed commit descriptions.</p>

questiontext.text: <p>If a TEI file passes validation in a student's local desktop editor but fails in the GitHub Actions CI runner, what is the most likely cause?</p>

answer.text: <p>Configuration drift: the local editor is validating against a different or outdated schema version compared to the pinned canonical schema running in CI.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Correct. Local IDEs often cache older schemas or use default configurations; CI provides the authoritative, reproducible baseline environment.</p>

answer.text: <p>GitHub's servers do not have access to electricity on weekends.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. GitHub operates 24/7 cloud data centers.</p>

answer.text: <p>The XML language changes its grammar rules every 24 hours at midnight.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. XML and TEI standards remain stable across years.</p>

answer.text: <p>The student used a Mac, and GitHub Actions only supports smartphones.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. GitHub Actions runs on enterprise Linux, Windows, and macOS virtual machines.</p>

name.text: 10 Question: Purpose of the Editorial Consolidation Milestone

questiontext.text: <p>Why is a dedicated consolidation milestone strategically valuable before transitioning to final publication and web rendering?</p>

answer.text: <p>It ensures that all previous editorial layers (cataloguing, transcription, collation, and linguistic parsing) are synchronized, validated, and free of syntax defects before building downstream publication pipelines.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Correct. Consolidation stabilizes the textual corpus, ensuring that downstream transformation and publication pipelines operate on clean, standardized, bug-free data.</p>

answer.text: <p>It allows students to permanently delete their manuscript witnesses and stop working.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. The consolidation phase prepares materials for final publication, not abandonment.</p>

answer.text: <p>It serves as a mandatory vacation during which all computer screens must be turned off.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. It is an active laboratory consolidation and validation period.</p>

answer.text: <p>It changes the course syllabus to eliminate all remaining deadlines.</p>

feedback.text: <p>Incorrect. Course schedules and publication deadlines remain in full effect.</p>
